1	# Repository and module layout
2	
3	Recorded 2026-09-10 from the user's agreement on repository organization, CLI
4	naming and the browser report. This chapter is the single current home for
5	those structural decisions and the remaining crate/package design. Its companion
6	file inventory owns the proposed target filenames and generates the tables below. It records
7	user-agreed direction; technical integration and independent review remain
8	pending. It grants no implementation readiness or authorization. The
9	[central register](08-decision-and-readiness-register.md#unified-product-design-readiness)
10	continues to own readiness.
11	
12	The [implementation boundaries and build plan](implementation-boundaries-and-build-plan.md)
13	owns the concrete API handoff, private recovery record/failure matrix,
14	generation/build rules, tooling decision matrix and source-bound milestone coverage.
15	The [prototype report inventory](prototype-report-inventory.md) owns its 24
16	feature dispositions. These focused companions extend this layout without
17	creating alternate readiness records; both are author proposals pending Claude.
18	
19	## Agreed organization
20	
21	Settle the major package boundaries before implementation. Each package needs a
22	clear responsibility, public interface, permitted dependencies and build output.
23	Individual source files and small internal module divisions can evolve within
24	those boundaries during implementation.
25	
26	The proposed product source tree is:
27	
28	```text
29	apps/
30	  cli/                  Command-line application and host assembly
31	  report/               Browser report interface, styles and assets
32	crates/
33	  reporting/            Host-owned report projection and HTML assembly
34	  contracts/            Shared inert contract types (proposed)
35	  identity/             Pure canonical admission and identities (proposed)
36	  evaluator/            Pure evaluation and semantic replay (proposed)
37	  syntax/               Pure grammar parsing and clone candidates (proposed)
38	  platform/             OS mechanisms (proposed)
39	  security/             Trust, custody and grants (proposed)
40	  storage/              Retained evidence mechanics (proposed)
41	  components/           Component supervision and protocols (proposed)
42	  lifecycle/            Install/update/recovery coordination (proposed)
43	  host/                 Host authority and workflows (proposed)
44	providers/
45	  typescript/           TypeScript/JavaScript provider
46	  rust/                 Rust provider and its toolchain boundary
47	schemas/                Owned wire contracts and binding generation
48	tests/
49	  conformance/          Shared contract and compatibility checks
50	  integration/          Complete workflows across component boundaries
51	  qualification/        Platform and performance evidence requirements
52	tools/                  Build, release and repository maintenance
53	docs/                   Current product and developer documentation
54	```
55	
56	This is the target organization for implementation. These directories have not
57	been scaffolded by this decision. It does not move the existing architecture
58	record or its pinned schema and evidence files. The initial inventory below
59	proposes crate boundaries and direct dependencies for review. Complete API,
60	workspace and build configuration decisions remain open.
61	
62	### CLI names
63	
64	Directory, Cargo package and installed executable have distinct purposes:
65	
66	| Item | Agreed name |
67	|---|---|
68	| Source directory | `apps/cli/` |
69	| Cargo package | `opensip-cli` |
70	| Installed executable | `opensip` |
71	
72	The CLI assembles and invokes host services. Its directory name does not move
73	semantic authority into argument parsing or presentation code.
74	
75	### Report ownership and delivery
76	
77	The browser report has its own source home at `apps/report/`. Report-specific
78	components, styles and browser assets stay together there. A generic
79	`packages/ui/` is reserved for a future demonstrated need to share visual
80	components between applications; it is not part of the initial package list.
81	
82	`crates/reporting/` owns preparation of host-approved report data and assembly
83	of the HTML output with its built assets. The inventory now proposes the Cargo
84	package name `opensip-reporting` and one renderer module per applicable output
85	format in that crate. Those refinements require technical review; only the
86	directory and report responsibility were agreed in the initial discussion.
87	
88	The responsibilities follow the existing
89	[workflow output contract](../contracts/product-v1/workflows-and-surfaces.md#8-command-inventory-outputs-and-parity-ar-13-surfaces-ar-16):
90	
91	1. The admitted analysis and host evaluation produce findings, evidence and
92	   assessments under their existing authority rules.
93	2. The host prepares the declared report projection. Reporting code preserves
94	   those values and assembles the deliverable.
95	3. The browser interface presents the embedded data. Any agreed filtering or
96	   navigation changes presentation, without recomputing policy or changing the
97	   underlying findings, evidence, verdict or completeness disclosures.
98	
99	The selected HTML deliverable remains a self-contained, offline file with its
100	data embedded and no script-fetched data. It requires no separately running
101	web server. Building `apps/report/` produces assets for that deliverable;
102	placing its source under `apps/` does not select a hosted service, server-side
103	rendering or a separate installation. The companion build plan now specifies exact asset-manifest and signed host
104	release-artifact joins under the offline delivery contracts; those corrected
105	bytes require review. No frontend framework or bundler is selected
106	by this directory decision.
107	
108	The prototype's source has now been inventoried at its pinned commit in the
109	[report inventory](prototype-report-inventory.md), with 24 proposed preservation,
110	or change dispositions and reasons. HTML output is selected; executed
111	feature parity and independent acceptance have not yet been established. Any
112	change to the current offline or data-access contract needs explicit review.
113	
114	## Rules for a maintainable repository
115	
116	- Give every contract and shared type one source owner. Generate language
117	  bindings or enforce explicit drift checks; do not maintain competing copies
118	  by hand.
119	- Document the allowed dependency direction and enforce it in repository
120	  checks. Preserve the pure evaluator's lack of effects and the host's
121	  authority over admission, lifecycle, persistence and outcomes.
122	- Create a crate when it establishes a useful dependency boundary, isolates
123	  substantial dependencies, or supports independent testing or delivery.
124	  Smaller responsibilities may remain internal modules. A directory does not
125	  imply a process, separately installed component or independent release.
126	- Define provider workspaces and toolchain requirements explicitly so unrelated
127	  provider dependencies do not become mandatory CLI build dependencies.
128	  Independent releases continue to use the common compatibility and packaging
129	  contracts; directory layout does not introduce lockstep versions.
130	- Keep unit tests near their implementation. Give shared fixtures,
131	  conformance checks, integration tests and qualification workloads explicit
132	  homes and owners. Reference fixtures do not become product qualification
133	  merely by being copied into a test directory.
134	- Maintain one current documentation reading path. Update the owning document
135	  as decisions evolve and use version control for its history. Keep retained
136	  audit/review evidence clearly identified and linked without duplicating the
137	  current design across successive status documents.
138	- Keep build outputs and temporary agent work out of the normal source tree.
139	  Generated bindings have the explicit locations below; the build plan proposes
140	  checking them in with byte-for-byte regeneration checks. Asset bundles remain
141	  build outputs. Generator/tool selection still requires review.
142	  Retain required review evidence deliberately with its own custody;
143	  existing frozen evidence is not deleted or reorganized by this decision.
144	
145	## File inventory and naming conventions
146	
147	The user requested an explicit directory/filename list with a description of
148	what belongs in each file, including consistent names for similar
149	implementations. The [machine-readable inventory](repository-file-inventory.v1.json)
150	is the source for the generated tables below. Edit its entries and regenerate
151	this section; do not maintain a second handwritten list. Proposed files become
152	real as their implementation is needed, with the inventory updated whenever a
153	reviewed split, merge or rename changes their responsibilities.
154	
155	These are initial structural proposals. A listed filename does not establish
156	that its API, algorithm, dependency selection or product qualification is done.
157	This inventory deliberately leaves tool-specific build configuration and the
158	full schema migration map open until their owning decisions are made. Shared
159	platform behavior remains host-owned even when its code is in a support crate.
160	
161	### Naming rules
162	
163	| Category | Rust | TypeScript | Meaning |
164	|---|---|---|---|
165	| Ordinary source module | `snake_case.rs` | `kebab-case.ts` | Name the concrete responsibility; exported Rust types and TypeScript classes/types may use `PascalCase` |
166	| Factory | `<subject>_factory.rs` | `<subject>-factory.ts` | Select and construct an implementation from explicit inputs; do not hide workflow execution, discovery or permission grants in construction |
167	| Incremental builder | `<subject>_builder.rs` when a dedicated builder implementation exists | `<subject>-builder.ts` on the same rule | Incrementally construct a value; a function that constructs a descriptor can remain in its domain module |
168	| Named boundary adapter | `<boundary>_adapter.rs` | `<boundary>-adapter.ts` | Translate one named external boundary into owned structures; concrete platform mechanisms may retain names such as `filesystem.rs` |

194	### Ownership and dependency constraints
195	
196	Within the pure layers, `contracts` has no internal dependencies, `identity`
197	may depend on `contracts`, and `evaluator` may depend on `identity` and
198	`contracts`. Reversing those edges is forbidden even if the graph is acyclic.
199	These crates may also use explicitly reviewed pure external libraries.
200	They have no OS, provider, store or report UI dependency. Platform code supplies
201	mechanisms; security, lifecycle and host code decide whether an operation is
202	lawful. Host finalization coordinates the authoritative application boundary.
203	The [commit API proposal](implementation-boundaries-and-build-plan.md#admission-and-authoritative-commit)
204	requires storage's facade to consume opaque evaluator `ReplayedRun` and security
205	`CommitSession` prerequisites bound to the exact target; raw ledger mutation and
206	receipt constructors stay private to storage. Storage therefore gains direct
207	evaluator and security dependencies. An ordinary DTO or success flag cannot
208	substitute for those prerequisites. The exact carrier/recovery join is proposed
209	there for Claude review; no implemented type-level or durability guarantee is
210	claimed by this inventory.
211	
212	Components owns framing, negotiated protocol shape and session supervision.
213	Host fact admission owns the returned evidence's joins to the selected source,
214	context and Plan. Replay independently checks the semantic obligations over
215	explicitly supplied data. This keeps lifecycle's use of component management
216	from assigning it responsibility for analysis admission.
217	
218	The Rust provider is a separately pinned workspace. Its shared contract/identity
219	source dependencies must be resolved reproducibly without pulling its compiler
220	integration into the host workspace. The TypeScript provider and report are
221	separate packages. Both consume their selected generated bindings; neither
222	imports the other's runtime code. Report assets are supplied by build/release
223	assembly to host reporting, not by a runtime dependency on a web server.
224	
225	The source dependency graph alone does not describe these integration edges:
226	
227	| Relationship | Required boundary |
228	|---|---|
229	| Schemas → Rust contracts, TS provider and report bindings | Registry records exact source IDs/digests, profiles, generator version/options, generated targets and semantic validator owners; generated types alone do not perform runtime admission |
230	| Host components ↔ separately released providers | Negotiated process protocols and authenticated release closures; no source imports of compiler implementations into the host |
231	| Rust provider → shared Rust contract/identity libraries | Reproducible pinned dependency resolution within its separate workspace, explicit compatible toolchains and selected wire surfaces; a path dependency must not inherit incompatible root workspace settings |
232	| Report build → host reporting → CLI release | Versioned asset bundle matches the embedded projection and is included in the signed offline release closure; provider-only builds need no report toolchain |
233	| Shared fixtures → package tests and executable integration harnesses | Each scenario has an executable owner and an independent expected result; qualification evidence retains its separate standing |
234	
235	Root TypeScript scripts coordinate packages without making a combined frontend
236	build a prerequisite for provider development. A provider-side SDK is not yet
237	selected: compare shared transport obligations before adding a package. Common
238	host supervision, authorization and outcome behavior remains host-owned either
239	way. CLI bootstrap initializes only the services required by the admitted command;
240	static linkage does not justify opening stores or providers for help/version.
241	
242	Derived indexes belong to storage mechanics and have a lifecycle separate from
243	retained evidence. Host query owns exact Run/view selection, bounded traversal
244	and truthful completeness. Loss or interruption of an index leads to rebuilding,
245	a supported retained-evidence fallback or an explicit unavailable result under
246	the selected contract, never an invented empty answer. No graph engine is chosen.
247

24	## Admission and authoritative commit
25	
26	### Decision: require independently minted prerequisites at the storage boundary
27	
28	A private host wrapper alone cannot prevent another Rust caller of a public
29	storage crate from submitting unverified records. Select two opaque prerequisites:
30	the pure evaluator produces a **ReplayedRun**, and security produces a live
31	**CommitSession**. Storage can publish an authoritative commit only with both,
32	bound to the same exact target. Host finalization remains the application
33	coordinator; it does not manufacture either prerequisite from booleans or DTOs.
34	
35	This changes the proposed source graph: `opensip-storage` depends directly on
36	`opensip-evaluator` and `opensip-security`, in addition to contracts, identity
37	and platform. Neither evaluator nor security depends on storage. Lifecycle may
38	continue to use storage without a reverse storage → lifecycle edge. Security also depends on the pure evaluator to accept its opaque `ReplayedRun`
39	at the SEAL boundary; a caller-authored RunId is insufficient. The evaluator
40	remains entirely pure; being called by effectful storage does not give it ports,
41	callbacks or access to live state. The dependency/footprint tradeoff is explicit
42	and requires Claude review. Do not create an extra admission crate merely to
43	hide this edge or weaken full replay to keep a diagram smaller.
44	
45	These are proposed Rust API type names, not new serialized contracts:
46	
47	| Type / operation | Constructor and visibility | Invariant |
48	|---|---|---|
49	| `RunCandidate` | Inert contract input; callers may construct/deserialize it | Makes no admission claim |
50	| `ReplayedRun` | Public opaque evaluator type; constructor private to complete replay in `replay.rs` | Contains exact admitted closure, recomputed RunId, retention inventory and selected profile after full semantic reconstruction; no `Default`, deserialization or unchecked constructor |
51	| `CommitSession` | Public opaque security type; created only by security admission over registered project/store custody, an owned live platform writer guard, actual grants and operation identity | Binds namespace, store generation, ExecutionId, admitted producer closure and permitted operation; acquisition never follows from a Run's semantic grant projection |
52	| `PreparedCommit` | Public opaque storage type; returned by `prepare_commit(ReplayedRun, CommitSession)` | Owns both prerequisites and the exact binding; checks equality and retention feasibility, then permits only the defined publication sequence |
53	| `PublishedCommit` | Public opaque storage result; constructor private to durable commit/recovery validation | Contains the exact committed receipt and Run reference after required barriers, not merely after writing blobs or appending SEAL |
54	| `RecoveredCommit` | Storage recovery result validated against current ledger and objects | Distinguishes confirmed commit, confirmed absence/failure and an inability to establish either; recovery does not repeat source mutation |
55	
56	Owned guards and commit state are single-use and non-cloneable. Immutable byte
57	buffers may be shared read-only; the opaque wrapper exposes no mutable interior
58	or references that let a caller replace a validated object. An owned byte arena
59	or pinned read-only verified object set can avoid copying the entire closure;
60	filesystem paths alone cannot freeze it. Accessors provide identities and
61	read-only values, never a way to construct the prerequisite. Test helpers that
62	skip admission remain private to unit tests and unavailable in release builds.
63	
64	`ReplayedRun` establishes semantic validity, not compiler truth, present custody
65	or current availability. `CommitSession` establishes operational admission, not
66	semantic validity. Storage compares their target identities, inventories and
67	producer selections, binds the current attempt and verifies all published bytes.
68	Changed Plan inputs require new replay. A new attempt using the same semantic
69	Run still requires a new session and its own ExecutionId/receipt.
70	
71	The storage crate exports read APIs, cache/index APIs, authorized maintenance
72	APIs and the guarded commit facade. SQL connections, transaction handles,
73	ledger-row insertion and receipt constructors remain private modules. Host,
74	lifecycle and CLI cannot obtain raw writable ledger access through a convenience
75	method. Maintenance cannot insert an authoritative Run by using a restore or
76	migration helper: imported evidence is revalidated before local adoption, and
77	state transitions retain their separate authorization and recovery laws.
78	
79	This is an API discipline inside the trusted host, not an OS sandbox or a
80	defense against arbitrary malicious native code running with store access.
81	Custody, exact-byte admission and actual platform qualification remain necessary.
82	
83	### Security/storage ownership and the final commit gate
84	
85	`begin_journal_txn(session: CommitSession)` consumes the session and returns an
86	opaque `JournalWriteTxn` owned by security. It owns the live session and its
87	operation lease, has no public SQL/write/checkpoint method and is non-cloneable.
88	It does not borrow a session that a later call must move. Storage holds this
89	opaque transaction while acquiring its own non-waiting level-3 ledger transaction.
90	Failure of that second acquisition calls the security-owned consuming abort path.
91	
92	`JournalSealBinding` is also defined and privately constructed in security,
93	not in the inert contracts crate. It exposes read-only actual carrier/generation,
94	SEAL sequence/body digest, operationRef and replayed Run identity. It is evidence
95	of that append, never a reusable effect grant. Storage owns the remaining receipt
96	and inventory values and assembles the thirteen-field association by checking
97	both owners' exact joins; security does not manufacture storage's receipt counter
98	or receipt bytes. Neither raw transaction handles nor the append mutex escape.
99	
100	The security-owned `seal_under_append_lock` consumes `JournalWriteTxn`, borrows
101	an evaluator-minted `ReplayedRun`, and owns the entire checkpoint/witness sequence.
102	It uses a two-phase storage adapter, whose concrete implementation and ledger
103	connection stay private to storage:
104	
105	1. After the SEAL/witness is durable, an at-most-once staging callback receives
106	   the opaque `JournalSealBinding`, validates its joins and inserts the exact
107	   receipt/association in the already-open evidence transaction. It returns an
108	   owned prepared-ledger-commit adapter. This phase may fail without issuing an
109	   evidence commit; it must not commit or publish by itself.
110	2. Security rechecks epoch/freshness and atomically admits commitment only if the
111	   observer's fail-stop latch has not won. It then consumes the adapter's one
112	   commit method. All payload admission, association construction and SQL staging
113	   precede this gate; the method performs only the prepared commit and barriers.
114	
115	The adapter trait is owned by security, which has no dependency on storage;
116	its implementation is storage-private. No authority-bearing type lives in
117	contracts merely to permit another crate to construct private fields. The trait
118	is an operational collaboration among trusted host modules, not a sandbox for
119	arbitrary downstream implementations. Storage's public facade accepts neither
120	an external adapter nor an external `SealOutcome`; callers cannot mint
121	`PublishedCommit` by returning a fabricated enum. The pure evaluator receives no
122	callback, port or mutable store handle.
123	
124	The observer latches fail-stop outside the append mutex when a check fails or
125	staleness exceeds S6’s bound. Use one atomic bit state with `ADMITTED=1` and
126	`LATCHED=2`: 0 is preparing, 1 admitted, 2 latched before admission, and 3 admitted
127	then latched. Commit admission uses compare-exchange 0→1; the observer always
128	fetch-ORs 2, including 1→3, so a post-admission latch cannot be lost. No state
129	resets during the attempt. The successful gate mints one internal single-use
130	permit for the already prepared commit; it is not a reusable grant for later
131	effects. State 3 does not revoke that already admitted attempt or relabel its
132	outcome: it records the latch and forbids further effect admission or retries.
133	A latch winning at state 0 prevents the gate entirely. The observer cannot undo
134	an in-flight syscall or rewrite its outcome. A confirmed durable commit remains committed; an uncertain
135	commit/barrier remains durability-undetermined with ExecutionId and no automatic
136	write retry. This gate orders admission only and is not the durability point.
137	
138	On any end path, security returns a stopped session that still owns the operation
139	lease and admits cleanup only, with no further analysis/effect APIs. After level 4
140	and any still-open ledger transaction are released, the host uses that stopped
141	session to record pending REV/cleanup through a fresh lawful level-3→level-4 append
142	while the operation lease still protects cleanup. It then releases the lease and
143	performs the ordinary S7 end handoff. Capacity exhaustion instead returns typed
144	`CarrierCapacityExhausted {grantGeneration, provenTailSeq}` through storage to
145	`host/finalization.rs`; after cleanup and lease release, host routes the required
146	lifecycle rollover under the fence. Storage never calls lifecycle backwards.
147	
148	The outer PreparedCommit state has no Drop implementation that prevents moving its owned fields during publish; best-effort rollback/release belongs to the inner guards and ledger transaction. Drop is best-effort rollback/resource release if it runs; `mem::forget`, process
149	abort and stalled syscalls do not guarantee destructor execution. Those paths
150	must leave recovery evidence and an honest unavailable/busy result, not a claimed
151	cleanup success. This design does not infer OS cancellation bounds from Rust types. Because cross-crate adapter traits are public, another trusted security caller could use its own adapter and leave an orphan SEAL without an evidence receipt. Such a SEAL consumes journal capacity and participates in witness/recovery accounting exactly as F36 requires; it cannot manufacture PublishedCommit through storage’s facade.
152	
153	### Publication sequence and lock discipline
154	
155	1. Host obtains registered project/store admission and the required writer guard
156	   through lifecycle/security before source admission. The guard remains owned
157	   through evaluation and commit. Operational grants precede Plan construction;
158	   Plan grant descriptors never authorize effects.
159	2. Native/import admission and the pure evaluator reconstruct the complete Run.
160	   A failed reconstruction returns its typed failure without producing
161	   `ReplayedRun`. Explicit ephemeral analysis uses a separate non-authoritative
162	   result path and cannot call the durable commit facade.
163	3. Storage binds the two prerequisites and preflights exact replayable retention,
164	   pins and bounds. It writes verified immutable objects to private temporary
165	   files, satisfies file barriers, publishes digest-addressed objects and
166	   satisfies directory barriers. Failure leaves no acknowledged Run.
167	4. Prepare both carrier write transactions at level 3 in one fixed order:
168	   security grant-journal first, evidence ledger second, both non-waiting. If
169	   either acquisition fails, release the earlier transaction. Only then take
170	   the journal append checkpoint at level 4. It never holds level 4 while
171	   trying to acquire either level-3 transaction. No lease upgrade or new project/fence
172	   acquisition occurs inside this path. Existing S7 rules own earlier fence and
173	   lease acquisition/release and contention handling.
174	5. Under the journal checkpoint, security checks current custody, relevant trust
175	   epoch, observer freshness, grants and operation cancellation. The final
176	   SEAL/commit sequence must linearize with REV: no new SEAL or commit after REV.
177	   No slow replay, provider execution, network operation or discovery occurs
178	   while this final lock is held. A short-lived checkpoint is never serialized
179	   as a reusable authority token.
180	6. Publish the Run manifest, references, availability, authorized pins, exact
181	   receipt and private recovery association in one synchronous ledger
182	   transaction; satisfy all required durability barriers. Only then produce
183	   `PublishedCommit`. Required rendering/delivery follows commitment and cannot
184	   rewrite its Run.
185	
186	**Proposed journal/ledger crash join for review:** persist the validated SEAL
187	record before ledger commit while holding the final journal lock through the
188	ledger commit/barrier. Include a private recovery association in that ledger
189	transaction linking namespace, ExecutionId, RunId, inventory digest, store
190	generation and the exact journal generation/sequence/record digest. Its values
191	come from the actual two owners, not caller assertions. The association is local
192	operational metadata, excluded from semantic hashes, and adds no field to the
193	closed public receipt or JournalRecord schemas. SEAL alone is not a durable
194	receipt. A surviving SEAL with no committed ledger row is an uncommitted attempt.
195	`admit_analysis_seal` validates a record and its Run; it does not establish that
196	attempt’s durable commitment. F36 requires the orphan attempt to remain
197	uncommitted after later operations. A later, properly receipted attempt may
198	commit the same semantic RunId; its new ExecutionId/receipt establishes that
199	commit and never retroactively confirms the earlier attempt.
200	
201	This is a concrete proposed carrier join, not a claim that candidate25 already
202	specifies or implements that private table. Claude must check its compatibility
203	with the selected journal carrier, operationRef binding, recovery and bounded
204	revocation rules. The private record shape and ordered fault-injection plan below now make the
205	proposal concrete. Their carrier implementation/migration still requires review
206	and real execution before qualification.
207	If that review requires a normative amendment, freeze and review a successor;
208	do not silently edit the selected public schemas or weaken the existing laws.

210	### Failure and recovery account
211	
212	| Interruption / refusal | Durable state and required behavior |
213	|---|---|
214	| Invalid closure or semantic mismatch | No replay prerequisite; no acknowledged Run or fabricated commit receipt |
215	| Wrong namespace/store generation, substituted Run/inventory or expired operational session | Refuse before authoritative publication; never repair the mismatch by rebinding an existing token |
216	| Object write/digest/barrier failure | No ledger commit; unreferenced blobs are reconciled under existing GC/custody rules |
217	| REV/cancellation/freshness failure before commit | Prevent subsequent SEAL/commit according to S6; disclose already completed effects under their own rules |
218	| Durable SEAL, ledger transaction not committed | No authoritative acknowledgement; recovery requires verified ledger absence before calling the attempt uncommitted; a read failure is not absence |
219	| Commit/barrier result uncertain, or acknowledgement lost | Return the existing durability-undetermined outcome with ExecutionId; read-only recovery checks the ledger, binding and objects; no automatic mutation retry |
220	| Receipt confirms commit, later object loss/corruption | Preserve historical sealed assurance and verdict; report current availability and missing references separately |
221	| Required report projection/rendering fails after commit | Preserve RunId; existing required-delivery operational failure/exit 4 applies |
222	| Optional browser launch/export fails | Disclose the optional delivery failure according to the selected surface; do not change the sealed result |
223	
224	Recovery must not use a lone SEAL, a matching cache key or a syntactically valid
225	RunId as proof of commitment. Conversely, revocation after a confirmed commit
226	does not erase history. Corrupt or contradictory operational records require
227	an honest recovery/custody failure under the owning error contract; this design
228	does not invent a new public error code to conceal an unmapped case.

230	### Private recovery record and storage-generation binding
231	
232	The machine-readable [recovery plan](commit-recovery-plan.v1.json) owns the closed
233	`CommitRecoveryAssociationV1` schema and F00–F53 checkpoint inventory. This is a
234	local operational record, never a public request, authority token or extension
235	to a Run/receipt/journal wire schema. All 13 fields are required, with no nulls,
236	unknown members, implicit defaults, duplicate JSON keys or lossy numeric parsing.
237	JSON Schema checks shape; the exact lexical and cross-owner checks below still
238	apply. Merely constructing a schema-valid association grants nothing.
239	
240	Select a private `StoreGenerationBindingV1` with exactly `{schemaVersion: 1,
241	namespaceId, storeInstanceId, storeGeneration, stateSchema}`. `namespaceId` is the same exact
242	1–4096-character registered namespace used by the receipt; `storeInstanceId`
243	is 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters from 128 bits of OS randomness allocated
244	once at authorized store creation. `storeGeneration` is exactly the S9.2
245	admitted `currentStoreGeneration` (`I64NonNegative`), validated against the
246	transition intent’s `from/toStoreGeneration`; it is not a second counter and it
247	is not monotonic, because S9.2 `store-rollback`/`core-rollback` re-select a
248	retained earlier generation. `stateSchema` uses the owning security
249	`$defs/StateSchema` domain, currently
250	`{1, 2}`. It widens only through an explicit reviewed successor of that owner
251	and supported-reader admission, never because a generic integer can encode it.
252	The binding is custody-protected store metadata; `storeGenerationDigest` is raw
253	SHA-256 over the exact canonical bytes produced by the one foundation
254	product-profile canonicalizer of identity §3, selected by security S2 because
255	this record carries a `schemaVersion`. It is a raw-artifact digest used only for
256	local correlation, never `H(domain, descriptor)`: it is not a new
257	public H-domain, semantic identity or proof that a store is trusted. The active
258	security guard obtains this binding through an admitted handle and registry,
259	not from request fields. Randomness never enters the pure evaluator or Run hash.
260	Adding any member would change every historical digest, so this record is frozen
261	at version 1; a new member needs a V2 plus a reviewed bridge that preserves the
262	original digests, never a silent in-place edit.
263	
264	The binding survives ordinary restart, a same-store core update that preserves
265	the admitted state schema/store generation, and index rebuild.
266	**Current S9 cannot express this validation, and this proposal does not pretend
267	otherwise.** `InstallationTransitionIntentV1` (11 members) and
268	`InstallationTransitionJournalV1` (20 members) are closed with
269	`additionalProperties: false` and carry no store instance identity, and S9.2's
270	`registry` is a `NamespaceList` of namespace strings. The minimal S9 owner
271	successor is therefore authored as an explicit normative insertion —
272	[two pure `+`-only hunks](store-instance-lineage.v1.json) that remove no line:
273	the explicit schema/store pair law into S9.2
274	itself, and a `### S9.3` section after it — and its
275	private lifecycle companion is specified in
276	[store-instance lineage](store-instance-lineage.v1.json): a private
277	`StoreLineageNodeV1` keyed by the admitted binding triple
278	`(storeInstanceId, storeGeneration, stateSchema)`, carrying its predecessor
279	triple and the creating `intentDigest` as evidence, written **after** the
280	transition journal record is durably `COMMITTED`, under the already-required
281	fence and exact `leaseSet`, adding no member to any closed public, signed or
282	namespace record and minting no D9 code. `intentDigest` is a semantic input
283	digest, not an attempt identifier, so it is evidence and never a key: a lawful
284	retry of a byte-identical intent after an abort writes a different triple or no
285	node at all. That successor must be frozen and
286	reviewed; it is not accepted here.
287	
288	A store instance identity is allocated once per physical store and never
289	rewritten. Which transitions write a node is read from the admitted intent's own
290	`from`/`to` values, never from the operation name. The owner's pair law makes
291	that decidable without consulting any stored record: for `core-update` and
292	`core-rollback` alike an unchanged schema keeps the store
293	(`TRANSITION.SAME_SCHEMA_KEEPS_STORE`) and a changed schema selects a different
294	one (`TRANSITION.SCHEMA_CHANGE_SELECTS_NEW_STORE`), `core-repair` keeps all
295	three, and both store operations require a schema change *and* a different
296	generation. So equal `to`/`from` generation and schema keep the same physical
297	store and write nothing; a **retreating** schema re-selects a retained ancestor
298	and also writes nothing; only an **advancing** schema materializes a new store,
299	allocates a fresh identity and writes one node. Deriving the case from the intent
300	rather than from stored ancestry is deliberate: a case read out of the node set
301	would let a damaged lineage reclassify a rollback as a forward selection.
302	
303	Every lookup identifies a node by its **full triple**, whose instance component is
304	read from the store-root **marker** of the store concerned — the newly
305	materialized store for a forward selection, the retained ancestor for a
306	re-selection, the unchanged store for a same-store operation. A numeric
307	generation pair never identifies a node, because a retained branch may lawfully
308	present the same pair as a fresh target; no global generation uniqueness is
309	asserted beyond the owner's own rules. `intentDigest` is evidence checked *on* the
310	selected node rather than a search key, since the record's own schema says it may
311	repeat.
312	
313	Reading a store root yields exactly one of three outcomes — **readable**,
314	**absent** (no root present) or **unreadable** (a root observed whose marker is
315	malformed) — and an unreadable marker is never read as absence. The requirement is
316	**phase-bound**: the store a transition comes from always exists, so its marker is
317	always required, but the *selected* store's marker is required only where the
318	owner settles the transition as committed. At `LEASED` and `PREPARING` a forward
319	target may not yet have been materialized, and after an abort an unpublished target may
320	already have been reclaimed by the GC census, so an absent target there is expected
321	and must never be turned into corruption.
322	
323	One admission law governs both publication and recovery: shape admitted by the
324	private record's **own closed schema**, paired nulls,
325	no self-reference, a predecessor that already exists at its exact triple, no
326	disagreeing duplicate primary key, and an acyclic chain reaching exactly one
327	lineage root — scoped to that chain, because an authorized restore or adoption

329	the target key is idempotent but **not** a short circuit: it is validated the same
330	way and simply writes nothing. A
331	refusal writes nothing.

333	Recovery applies that **same** case and that same admission law, and only after

354	A rollback that re-selects the **same retained physical old store** keeps that

420	### Witness-aware publication and read-only recovery
421	
422	The inherited security v8 §5.4 witness protocol is part of the carrier boundary.
423	Final SEAL publication must complete its **PENDING witness → journal transaction
424	commit/barrier → COMMITTED witness** sequence before the evidence-ledger commit.
425	The broad journal record schema's i64 `seq` allowance does not override the
426	carrier's uint53 cap or reserved terminal slot: ordinary SEAL uses at most
427	`9007199254740990`; slot `9007199254740991` remains TERMINAL. Capacity handling
428	must finish through lifecycle outside the held operation lease, never by taking
429	its fence backwards inside commit.
430	
431	The inherited `security-schemas.v2/grant-journal.sql` does not admit SEAL in its
432	record-type CHECK and still names historical platform aliases. It is historical
433	carrier evidence, not ready-to-use product DDL. **COV-03** requires an explicitly
434	versioned product carrier migration that admits current schema-3 SEAL/current
435	platform records while preserving historical row interpretation, append-only
436	hash chains, reserved capacity, witness/high-water checks and the S9 reader/core
437	bridge. Do not disable SQL checks or relabel old rows as current.
438	**COV-03 resolved (proposed, not accepted):** the versioned carrier is
439	`docs/coop/design-corrections/security/carrier-format.v3.md` with DDL
440	`grant-journal.carrier.v3.sql` and dispatch `carrier-dispatch.v3.json`, selected by security
441	§S1 and bridged by §S9. It adds `carrierFormat` as an axis distinct from `recordSchema` and
442	`stateSchema`, carries TERMINAL as the frozen recordSchema-1 body so schema 3 is not widened,
443	uses the four S8 machine ids, and migrates additively. The inherited carrier is incompatible
444	in exactly two ways, both measured: the `SEAL` record type, and the three alias-only machine
445	platform ids on a GRANT. Eight of the nine schema-3 operational record types insert cleanly. A journal's own
446	SQLite transaction is distinct from the evidence ledger transaction; holding
447	the prescribed lock order does not make the two databases atomically committed.
448	The proposal orders both level-3 write transactions before the level-4 append
449	lock: grant journal, then evidence ledger. Every journal writer, including the
450	revocation observer, must use the same security-owned transaction-before-append
451	API; no caller may acquire a new journal transaction from inside an append-lock
452	callback. A failed second acquisition rolls back/releases the first. Committing
453	the journal releases its DB transaction while the append lock stays held through
454	the witness and evidence commit; no journal transaction is reacquired there.
455	Claude must review this refinement against S7 and every inherited journal writer.
456	
457	Read-only recovery may inspect a consistent ledger snapshot and the admitted
458	carrier/witness/floor state. It must not perform witness INIT, REVERT or ADVANCE,
459	raise trust high-water, allocate a store binding or obtain a new execution grant.
460	If reconciliation of the requested attempt's carrier prefix is needed, report
461	the owner diagnosis and inability to confirm current local custody; an
462	authorized lifecycle open performs the lawful mutation,
463	then a new read-only recovery can retry. The exact bounded algorithm is
464	`docs/v2/architecture/commit-recovery-readonly.v3.md`. Carrier observations are captured with
465	before/after stability brackets and at most one fresh journal retry; an owner quarantine
466	condition is reportable only from stable brackets plus two agreeing tail observations, so a
467	temporally skewed observation is attributed to busy rather than corruption. Terminality of an
468	attempt comes from the ledger-owned `AttemptCustodyV1` phase read in the same snapshot as the
469	receipt, never from an in-memory active set. A confirming result is
470	`confirmed-under-retained-custody`, never a cryptographic proof of the interior prefix. A mere absent or malformed witness never
471	licenses repair. The ordinary writer lifecycle's existing start/end high-water
472	handoff stays separate from a read-only request.
473	
474	A journal tail ahead of the witness, a missing witness for nonempty history,
475	a lower-than-observed tail, an equal sequence with different hash, unknown schema
476	or contradictory receipt/association is a custody/recovery refusal. A verified
477	empty exact ledger lookup can establish that an attempt did not commit; an
478	unreadable ledger, another generation, the requested attempt still running or
479	an unresolved witness for its required prefix cannot. Active-attempt recovery
480	may report in-progress/undetermined and must not declare a final failure from an
481	older read snapshot. A valid later append's PENDING witness does not invalidate
482	an earlier committed receipt: snapshot readers verify its retained durable
483	prefix and never wait for the writer or repair the newer witness. Ordinary
484	historical queries do not reuse current execution grants or turn each read into
485	whole-carrier recovery.
486	
487	Preserve the recovery association, exact receipt, store-generation lineage and
488	required journal verification material while their local commitment is retained.
489	They are operational custody state under G19, not disposable indexes. Removing
490	or compacting a journal generation requires an explicitly reviewed retained
491	verification bridge; absence of that bridge prevents deletion. This proposal
492	does not alter immutable assurance or claim that purge deletes exported copies.
493	
494	Before the atomic commit-admission gate, recheck the observer latch and
495	freshness/cancellation after any blocking journal/witness or association-staging
496	operation. SEAL may already be durable; a failed final checkpoint
497	latches fail-stop and rolls back the still-uncommitted evidence transaction.
498	Release the append lock and remaining carrier transaction resources before a
499	fresh lawful journal append records REV/cleanup under the stopped operation
500	lease, then release that lease and perform the S7 end handoff; never
501	reacquire a level-3 journal transaction under level 4. No further effect is
502	admitted from the failed session. The old SEAL remains an uncommitted attempt. The journal lock
503	orders REV against commit; it cannot bound an OS syscall stalled indefinitely.
504	S6 scheduling assumptions and real platform measurements remain required.

524	### Ordered failure matrix
525	
526	Conclusions below are internal scenario expectations, not new public D9
527	codes. An unreadable or contradictory observation always prevents an
528	uncommitted/committed conclusion. A missing receipt alone is not terminal
529	absence: that requires settled+refused and both receipt and association
530	absent in one coherent snapshot. No crash case has been executed.
531	
532	| Case / interruption | Possible stored state | Expected conclusion and action |

535	| F01 — Replay refuses or target/inventory is substituted | No authoritative receipt | refused: Neither structural-only validation nor a stale boolean/token can publish authority. |
536	| F02 — During temporary object write | Partial private temp files; no ledger receipt | unknown-attempt-open: Do not expose partial objects; later authorized reconciliation may remove orphans. |
537	| F03 — After temp write, before file barrier completes | Temporary bytes may or may not survive | unknown-attempt-open: Never infer durability from write return alone. |
538	| F04 — After object file barrier, during digest-addressed publication | Some immutable objects may be present | unknown-attempt-open: Verify existing collisions by exact digest/length; never overwrite unequal bytes. |
539	| F05 — After object publication, before directory barrier completes | Visible names may not survive restart | unknown-attempt-open: No receipt has committed; presence alone grants no authority. |
540	| F06 — After object barriers, journal/evidence transaction acquisition refused or busy | Durable orphan objects; no ledger receipt | unknown-attempt-open: Acquire journal then evidence level-3 transactions before append lock; if either acquisition fails release earlier resources, apply S7 non-waiting rules and preserve orphan status. |
541	| F07 — After witness PENDING persist, before SEAL journal transaction | Witness may lead journal tail by one | unknown-attempt-open: Read-only diagnosis reports would-REVERT; only authorized lifecycle open reconciles it. |

An unreadable ledger remains unknown-custody. |

Leave unresolved custody admitted for the authorized sweep; no automatic write retry. |

551	| F17 — Optional browser launch/export fails after required delivery | Committed Run and required artifact remain | committed: Optional effect failure is disclosed without rewriting result or treating export as required. |

615	## Build, generation and dependency rules
616	
617	### Independently selectable build lanes
618	
619	| Lane | Source roots and prerequisites | Output / isolation requirement |
620	|---|---|---|
621	| Host libraries and CLI development | Root Cargo workspace: `apps/cli` and selected `crates/*`; root lockfile/toolchain | Native host and package tests; neither provider compiler integration nor Node/report build is an implicit Cargo build-script prerequisite |
622	| Rust provider | Separate `providers/rust` workspace, lockfile and toolchain; exact shared pure library sources | Provider executable plus its declared runtime/compiler/standard-library assets; host build does not compile rustc integration |
623	| TypeScript provider | Its own TS package and pinned compiler/runtime dependencies | Provider executable/launch payload and sealed runtime closure; no browser/report imports or frontend build requirement |
624	| Browser report | `apps/report` and generated projection binding | Self-contained asset bundle and compatibility descriptor; no provider or host runtime imports |
625	| Contract generation | Selected schema source registry and pinned generator closure | Rust/TS carriers, TS runtime shape validation and module indexes; deterministic drift check across every declared output |
626	| Product release assembly | Explicitly chosen native binaries, report assets, providers, storage and trust inputs | Signed exact offline closure and compatibility/TCB inventory; source directory adjacency does not establish compatibility |
627	
628	The default product release remains authoritative-capable. A management-only
629	installation is explicit and refuses analysis until its required signed closure
630	is installed through the authorized lifecycle. Optional development build lanes
631	must not become a new preview product, silently omit required capabilities from
632	a release, or download missing tools at runtime.
633	
634	**Rust workspace policy.** Shared pure packages must be usable from the pinned
635	provider workspace without accidentally inheriting the root workspace's compiler
636	or dependency settings. Their distributable manifests explicitly resolve package
637	metadata and dependencies; source-package assembly may materialize inherited
638	values, but the isolated provider build must prove they resolve without the host
639	workspace. Each workspace's lockfile is authoritative for that build. Shared
640	library/API compatibility, each wire major and toolchain support are separate
641	axes; a new host release does not force a provider release. Build inputs may
642	include immutable exported source packages from the one owner; never maintain
643	editable provider copies of shared contracts.
644	
645	**TypeScript policy.** Root scripts may coordinate the provider and report, but
646	must expose independent build/test targets. Select one package manager and
647	lockfile strategy before scaffolding; do not check in competing lockfiles. A
648	shared lockfile is acceptable only if each lane can install/build its declared
649	closure without running the other's scripts or requiring its toolchain. Provider
650	Node and browser DOM environments have separate compiler settings. Runtime
651	imports, type-only imports and generated inputs all appear in dependency checks;
652	type-only imports cannot hide duplicate schema ownership.
653	
654	**Generation policy.** Select checked-in generated bindings for the initial
655	implementation: ordinary builds can consume reviewed bindings without running a
656	generator or fetching schemas. Generated headers identify their owner and recipe;
657	the registry pins source digest/ID/profile, generator version/closure and options,
658	output target and semantic validator owner. The generation lane regenerates into
659	a clean temporary directory and compares bytes with the checked-in outputs.
660	Changes to a source/recipe must update every affected consumer in the same change.
661	Only explicit registry membership determines outputs; no glob over historical
662	schema versions. Generators must not resolve remote references implicitly.
663	
664	**Asset policy.** Generated JS/CSS bundles and release binaries are build outputs,
665	not checked-in application source. Report assembly emits a manifest of exact
666	asset bytes, projection compatibility and license/notice inputs. The host consumes
667	that manifest through an explicit build/release input; a Cargo build script must
668	not invoke an ambient package manager or contact the network. A source build can
669	use locally built assets; a verified prebuilt bundle is another explicit input.
670	Development host tests may use labelled fixture assets. A product release must
671	fail assembly if its selected report asset bundle is missing or incompatible.
672	Rendering a required output fails honestly if the installed assets are unusable.

676	Select pure `crates/syntax`, depending only on contracts and identity, with an
677	explicit host → syntax dependency. It takes immutable admitted source and grammar
678	bytes and returns inert candidates. It performs no filesystem discovery, compiler

722	
723	Select `{schemaVersion: 1, sources, recipes}` as the closed registry. A source row
724	has exactly `{sourcePath, sourceSha256, schemaId, declaredMajor, profile,
725	semanticValidatorOwner}`. Its path names a canonical repository-relative regular
726	file; sourceSha256 is raw SHA-256 of the complete exact document, not a fragment

728	the selected source owner. If the document has no such declaration, record the

733	A recipe row has exactly `{recipeId, generatorClosureSha256, optionsPath,

735	a hermetic generator closure and exact options-file bytes by lowercase SHA-256.

737	single output may depend on several schema documents without duplicate output
738	ownership. All transitive schema references must resolve within the recipe’s

740	registry bytes themselves are also an explicit generation input, enabling module

743	`outputs` is a nonempty path-sorted list of closed `{path, language, roles}` rows.

745	`carrier`, `shape-validator`, `module-index`. Each output path is globally unique
746	and belongs to its declared consumer’s generated directory. The initial recipe

753	sources, but never write the same output or read another recipe’s undeclared
754	outputs. Their exact inputs and own module-index populations remain explicit.

756	Every generated inventory path must occur exactly once in these output rows;
757	there are no exceptions for index modules or files combining roles. Regenerate

761	generated shape checking never proves lexical canonicalization, content identity

772	that pin before admitting the listed assets.

22	def ck(name, ok, detail=''):
23	    checks.append({'check': name, 'pass': bool(ok), 'detail': str(detail)[:400]})

31	def _no_dup(pairs):
32	    seen = set()
33	    for k, _ in pairs:
34	        if k in seen:
35	            raise ValueError('DUPLICATE KEY: ' + k)
36	        seen.add(k)
37	    return dict(pairs)

39	
40	def sload(path):
41	    """Strict JSON admission: reject duplicate object keys instead of taking the last value.
42	
43	    json.load is last-wins, so a file carrying two `admitted` keys parses cleanly and every
44	    assertion about the surviving value is silently about only one of them. Every selected JSON
45	    file in this correction is admitted through here.
46	    """
47	    with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as fh:
48	        return json.load(fh, object_pairs_hook=_no_dup)

2	
3	An internal refusal is not itself a public D9 code. The host retains the originating boundary and applies the public route for that boundary. It does not infer origin from a filename, a retained-versus-live flag or a prefix in the error text. The closed condition/origin routes are in evaluator-fault-observation.schema.v3.json. 4	
5	The same reference admission can be invoked over newly returned producer data or retained data. Re-admitting retained producer data preserves the producer-contract meaning of a structural violation. A known external configuration remains external configuration. A host bug constructing its own internal layer is a host invariant fault, as in the inherited native public-route law.
6	
7	| Condition | Public meaning |
8	| --- | --- |
9	| Malformed external policy, emission selection or configuration | request-rejected, CONFIG.INVALID, existing CONFIG.INVALID detail |
10	| Well-formed prospective selection above a published limit | request-rejected, REQUEST.UNSATISFIABLE; exact field/count/limit and narrowing remedy, before any Plan is minted |
11	| Invalid host-generated internal layer | operational-failed, SYSTEM.OUTCOME.ILLEGAL_STATE, host-invariant, existing HOST.INVARIANT_VIOLATED envelope detail |
12	| Provider omits a required inventory/result pointer, supplies a malformed outcome, or violates its Plan/stage/subject joins | operational-failed, PROVIDER.PROTOCOL_VIOLATION, provider-protocol; structural producer violation, including re-derivation over retained producer inputs |
13	| Referenced promised retained bytes are lost | the existing EvidenceUnavailable carrier: operational-failed, HOST.IO_FAILURE, host-io, evidence.missing plus the missing reference |
